translations.text: March 7. The life and suffering of the holy fathers who were bishops, Basil
and Capiton, who were martyred in Cherson. May Christ begin my discourse, he who alone is wise
and guides the wise. For both I and my words are in his hand.
Living and moving in him, then, take heed, you who are called by my name.
Do not close your ears because of my weakness, but for the sake of him who heals our weaknesses,
you should instead open your ears wide. Lay aside all distress and courageously understand what is being said. For it is not [?]
some contrived or deceitful thing that I ask your ears to hear, but for the sake of the true Word,
not words scattered into the air, but the very Word, the Son of God, through whom all things came into being,
those in heaven and those on earth, visible and invisible. He took upon himself the form of a servant,
yet did not cease to be God, but became flesh from the holy Virgin, the Mother of God.
Confess him as both God and man, wholly possessing what is his and wholly possessing what is ours,
God the Word, who suffered in the flesh and, as God, rose again in the flesh,
ascended into heaven, sat at the right hand of the Father, and raised us up with himself
in the hope of eternal life. He proclaimed this clearly in the words of the Gospel.
For he said, “Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.” Healing Thomas’s unbelief,
he left the hope of eternal life to the more courageous. But since these things, and others like them
contained in the Gospel, in profound old age and easily curable [?],
were sown in human minds so as to bear fruit thirtyfold,
sixtyfold, and a hundredfold, come forward, placing your neck under the yoke of him who took upon his shoulder
the death-dealing and deadly cross, so as thereby to fill the world above.
But since the ocean of wisdom is unfathomable, I ask you now to lend me your ears here,
so that I may praise the most glorious men, who through their sufferings shared in him who willingly suffered for us,
having enjoyed that honor and glory of the Lord.
For the things of God, recalled in God, gladden the heart. And what did he say? If
as Solomon says at greater length, having received a prophecy from God.
He said in Proverbs: “From the greatness and beauty of created things, one may perceive by comparison
how their Creator made them.” For the beauty of creation is truly to offer oneself blameless to God.
In agreement with this, the chosen vessel, the teacher of all nations, also said:
“You are the church of God, and the Spirit of God lives in you.”
How, then, would it not be fitting to think such things of these men, who poured out their own blood for humankind,
in imitation of the true shepherd, Jesus Christ our Lord? But what do I wish to say?
Let this true statement assure you: not even a small part
can be expressed here in praise of the holy and most honorable men who suffered martyrdom.
Nevertheless, putting their prayers in place of much worldly learning,
I will attempt, through their holiness, which brings healing to what is ailing within me,
to set forth things beneficial to the soul and establish a truthful remembrance of them for those who listen,
but to the praise and glory of the holy fathers themselves and the martyrs in the city of Cherson,
the God-loving and faithful men who lived there. For during the persecution under the impious Diocletian,
while the life-giving word of the Christian faith was at work,
as he himself had said, “Behold, I send you out like lambs among wolves,”
it happened to that most splendid of Jerusalem’s luminaries in the holy church,
who was in that very church of the Lord,
in the years of Diocletian, that this holy
bishop fell into trouble in the sixteenth year of Diocletian’s reign,
as he devoted great effort, labor, and zeal
to spreading the God-given word of the blameless Christian faith,
never ceasing to send bishops into all the lands of the nations.
I mean the holy bishop, [?] the pagan lands, and here also, to the city of Cherson,
in the land of Taurica, by the name of Basil. When he arrived
and saw the prevailing pagan deception, he began to teach the men of the city, saying:
For those whom you consider gods, possess, and honor are not gods, but idols unable to help you. For there is a God in heaven,
who created all things by his word and, by his wisdom,
brought all things from nonexistence into existence, and by his Holy Spirit
gives life to all. We worship him in the Holy Trinity and glorify him.
When the men of that city heard this from the holy man, they rushed to insult and beat him,
refusing to listen to him because of the senselessness caused by the delusion that held them.
Therefore the holy bishop stayed in a secluded place, living in a cave called the Maiden’s Cave.
But the most merciful God, who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth,
did not allow the whole city and its land to perish through Satan, but planted his Holy Spirit within them.
For this reason he also clothed himself in flesh and willingly endured crucifixion on the cross,
to set everyone free by his precious blood.
Through that blood, this city of Cherson too sought to be saved along with all the others, as he worked miracles. And there occurred
the following miracle. A certain man appointed as a leader of that city had an only son.
When the son died, they buried him outside the city. His parents happened to remain beside the body of their dead son
and fell asleep at his grave while weeping. Immediately, in a dream, they saw their son saying to them:
“Why do you weep and lament over my death? You cannot receive me back alive,
because your gods cannot do this, being lifeless stones and idols,
which the devil made to deceive and destroy people. But if you want to receive me back alive,
beg that stranger whom you beat and insult,
and believe in the God whom he proclaims. For he is able to raise me from the grave
through that man’s prayer.” When these things had been said to them in their dream,
they both awoke and told one another the vision of the dream, each giving an account that agreed with the other’s.
When day came, they entered the city and told their relatives what they had seen during the night.
They received the news joyfully and began looking for the holy bishop. When they found him in the cave
where he was praying, they fell down before him, saying, “We beg you, give us our son.”
But he said to them, “How can I do this, being a sinful man? But if you believe in the God whom I proclaim,
then he will raise your dead son for you.” They said to him, “Let us have our son back alive,
and we will do whatever you say.” The holy bishop went with them, taking the supplies for his episcopal ministry.
Carrying also what was needed for holy baptism, they came to the tomb.
They rolled away the stone and entered the tomb, where their dead son lay.
The holy bishop made the sign of the cross and sighed, and laid his hand on the dead man.
He said the prayer of life-giving baptism over his body.
As though over a living person, he poured consecrated water over the body, invoking the Holy Trinity.
Immediately the dead man rose. When his parents saw him,
they fell at Saint Basil’s knees, begging him to baptize them too.
After instructing them in the faith, he immediately granted them holy baptism and communion in the immortal mysteries.
They returned home and rejoiced with their whole household, having believed in the Lord.
But the devil, seeing himself gradually being deserted, defeated by the holy man’s arrival,
planted an arrow in the Jews whom he had deceived, so that they would stir the pagans to anger
and dare to kill the holy man. They came to the cave where the holy bishop lived,
found him, and bound him by the feet, and dragged him along the city street.
When they reached the place where Christians have now erected a pillar bearing the life-giving cross,
the holy bishop gave up his soul. They dragged his body outside the gates called Hiera,
and, having dragged it out, threw it down for the dogs to eat. It lay there for many days,
but God’s providence did not abandon the holy man’s body even after death.
At night a wolf would sit beside the body to guard it,
while two bright stars shone over the place where it lay; by day an eagle performed the same
task. Then those who had come to believe in Christ through this most holy man, because of the fear hanging over them
from the great number of pagans, buried his holy body at night,
outside the walls, to the west of the city, close to that same wall, on the seventh day of the month of March.
celebrating his memory with honor, to the glory of God Almighty. Amen.
A certain man who had been with the holy martyr Basil departed after his death
for the regions of the Hellespont. There he found other bishops who had then been sent by the holy bishop
for the same work of faith. He told them everything that had happened. When they heard this, they earnestly glorified God,
through whom Saint Basil had eagerly received the crown of martyrdom
by confessing Christ. And after consulting together—I mean Eugenius,
Agathodorus, and Elpidius—the venerable bishops went to that city of Cherson,
teaching in accordance with the true faith and following Saint Basil’s example.
The number of believers increased every day. But the devil, the ancient evildoer against the race of the faithful, was envious
and roused against them the Jews and Greeks who believed in him. They bound the holy men,
Eugenius, Agathodorus, and Elpidius, and dragged them along, beating them to death with clubs and stones.
They dragged the saints’ dead bodies out through the gates and threw them on the eastern outskirts,
so that dogs would eat them. But out of zeal for the baptism that brings salvation,
the Christians carried away their holy bodies and buried them on the sixth day of the month of December,
commemorating them to the glory of God Almighty. After a long time,
a bishop named Aetherius was sent there from Jerusalem.
While he was aboard a ship on his way to the aforementioned city, he was caught by a contrary wind
and driven onto an island called Alsos, in the region of the Dnieper River.
He fell ill with a severe disease, and, as he was about to depart this life, he prayed to the Lord, saying,
“Lord my God, though I am unworthy, you have granted me the honor of being appointed bishop. Do not leave me without remembrance in the city of Cherson.”
When he died, the faithful erected a great pillar at his grave.
Trees also grew up, marking his grave from afar.
After a long time, when the persecution of Christians by the lawless had passed,
the Romans appointed an emperor named Constantine, whom divine illumination
led into the wondrous light of Christianity.
And he issued an edict that anyone who did not confess the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit
should miserably lose his wicked life, and his house should be plundered. When these things had thus been piously decreed
concerning an end to the persecution of Christians, the faithful people of Cherson learned
of this command of the pious emperor and sent messengers to him, asking him to give them a bishop,
telling him everything about the miracles that had been performed by the holy fathers.
When the emperor heard these things from them, he rejoiced greatly and gave them a bishop named Capiton,
giving him five hundred soldiers who were believers.
With them the archbishop came to the city of Cherson at noon, through the providence
of God, who desires to save the human race.
As everyone was outside the city, the Christians received him with great joy.
Taking him along with those who were with him, they occupied the city walls.
Afterward, when the people of Cherson learned what had happened and come to pass, they gathered together and came to the wall.
They heard the bishop speaking to them as follows: “My children, I have not come to bring about your destruction,
but rather so that through faith in our Lord Jesus Christ you may receive salvation.” When peace had been established between the two sides,
all the people entered the city. The next morning, when everyone had gathered,
the bishop began to teach them the Christian faith, just as the bishops and martyrs before him had done.
But they answered him with words like those of the Athenians of old,
who answered the apostle Paul: “You are bringing some strange things to our ears.”
They said to him, “We have two kilns, constantly burning to make lime for the construction of our temple.
So pray to the God whom you worship, and enter them while they are burning.
And if you come out of the fire unharmed,
we will believe in the God whom you proclaim.” The bishop said,
“In the name of Jesus Christ my God, I will do this, and God will do this as you demand. But how am I to trust you that you will believe?
If you are willing, hand over your children to the soldiers, so that if you do not begin to believe in the faith of Christ,
they may be thrown into the kiln.” Everyone agreed to this proposal. Then the bishop approached one of the burning kilns.
After praying and making the sign of the cross over himself and the furnace he was about to enter, the deacon
having said, “Let us attend,” he entered the burning furnace and remained there a long time.
He poured some of the coals into the fold of his garment and came out unharmed and whole by the power of the Holy Spirit.
And they were greatly astonished and fell face down on the ground, glorifying the God of the Christians
and asking him to make them worthy of the holy Christian faith.
Therefore the faithful, filled with boundless joy,
prayed that Christian life might flourish among them. The holy bishop himself,
[?], instructed the men, together with their wives and children, in the faith, urging them to come sincerely to Christ.
And he made a baptismal font from the burnt lime from which he himself had been preserved unharmed.
There he baptized them all. Their Christian sponsors and fathers were the faithful of that city
and the soldiers who had come with that holy bishop himself. And they rejoiced with their entire households,
devoting themselves to prayer and to receiving the holy body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ,
and hastening every day to the holy bishop’s spiritual teaching.
Near that baptismal font they built a church of the holy and chief apostle Peter.
The holy bishop reported to the devout Emperor Constantine
the miracles worked by God in the city of Cherson, both before his time and during it.
The God-loving emperor received the letters that had been brought to him while he himself was together with the holy council
in the city of Nicaea in Bithynia, assembled against Arius, the enemy of Christ.
He thanked God and also reported to the holy council of 318 fathers
the miracles that God had worked in the city of Cherson during his reign
there. At the request of that holy bishop, there was sent to live permanently in the city of Cherson
Theonas, commander of five hundred soldiers, who had come there together with Saint Capito.
He set aside the eastern part of the city for them to live in. For this reason the people of Cherson called them “the foreign clan of Theonas.”
They all assembled and together departed from the district called the Small Marketplace
to the place called the Parthenon, those who were to live with the bishop and Theonas. Thus it has remained to this day.
drawing near, from the first and chief apostle Peter.
They are called Theonina. This, honored brothers, is the path and assurance of salvation.
The Savior of all, Christ our God, left us the lives of our holy martyrs and archbishops.
For what did they leave out of their words of instruction? And what deed did they not make known under the yoke?
Having lived their lives according to God's commandments and waged war against soul-destroying idols,
they left a memory that brings healing and is beneficial to life.
For they valued eternal life in heaven above the illusion of worldly glory, and they love and cherish it.
Not only during their lives, but also after death, having put death to death through their union with God,
having scorned the oil of sinners, the sanctification of their bodies,
they do not refuse to show mercy to those who run to them. For, having rightly confessed the Holy Trinity,
and having taught the most worthy to confess it rightly, those who run to them, through union with them,
they make citizens of heaven, themselves living with the angels.
Thus the city of Cherson has now become most glorious, instead of purple and scarlet,
having adorned itself with the blood of the holy fathers and archbishops, and having made [?] of stone that cannot be cut on either side,
against heretics and enemies—the tombs of the holy fathers, strong guards against all adversaries and [?].
But they also strike the demonic hosts through Christ's power.
Crying out to them, we pray that we may share with them in the kingdom of heaven,
through the grace and love for humanity of Christ our God, to whom belong glory and dominion for endless ages upon ages.
